opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

I usually think about AI in three layers, and the first two are the ones you're asking about. The first is information intelligence. That's AI that works in the digital world: language, search, recommendation, content generation, the large models we've all been talking about for the last few years. The data is mostly text, images, video and code, and the output is also information. When it makes a mistake, it writes a wrong sentence or gives a bad recommendation. That's annoying, but it can usually be corrected.

The second layer is physical intelligence. Here AI leaves the screen and acts in the real world, in autonomous vehicles, robots, drones, factories, and eventually humanoid robots. The intelligence has to perceive a messy, three-dimensional environment, understand physics, plan, and then act through hardware in real time. This is much harder for a few reasons. The data is scarcer and more expensive to collect, because you can't just crawl the internet for driving corner cases or robot manipulation. The long tail is very long. And safety requirements are on a completely different level. If a chatbot hallucinates, you get a funny answer. If a car hallucinates, someone can get hurt. So you need redundancy, verification, and often vehicle-road-cloud coordination rather than relying on a single model.

The third layer, which I think will matter more and more, is biological intelligence. That means AI connected to the human body and to life sciences: brain-computer interfaces, AI for drug discovery, protein design, and eventually intelligence that interacts directly with biological systems.

These three stages build on each other. The breakthroughs in information intelligence, especially foundation models and multimodal models, are now flowing into physical intelligence. Robots and cars can draw on world knowledge, reasoning and language, and the field is moving toward vision-language-action models and world models that can simulate physics. I'd describe it like this: information intelligence is already crossing the threshold of large-scale adoption, physical intelligence is approaching its "GPT moment" over the next several years, with autonomous driving likely to be the first truly large-scale embodied AI, and biological intelligence is further out but potentially the most profound.

So the difference isn't only about the type of data. It's about the cost of errors, how closely the system is coupled to the real world, and how fast it can iterate. That's why I believe the next decade will be about bringing AI from bits to atoms, and then to molecules and cells.

r001.rationale: The response describes information intelligence as AI working in the digital world, but does not compare it to human IQ.

r002.rationale: It says physical intelligence leaves the screen to act in the real world and must perceive and interact with its environment through hardware.

r003.rationale: It does not predict exceptionally high intellectual competence across fields within five years.

r004.rationale: It says physical intelligence is approaching a “GPT moment” over the next several years, but gives no estimate of about ten years for humanoid robots to reach a high level of physical intelligence.

r005.rationale: It does not predict that physically intelligent systems will outperform humans at most tasks in about ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
I usually think about AI’s development in three stages, and the first two are exactly the ones you’re asking about.

The first is information intelligence. This is everything happening in the digital world: text, images, voice, video, code. The large models we see today, from ChatGPT to Gemini to the Chinese models, are essentially information intelligence. They learn from data that already exists on the internet and in books, and they produce outputs that stay in the digital domain. The remarkable thing is how fast this has moved. In many tasks, language understanding, translation, writing, even reasoning, these models have reached or surpassed average human level. The reason it moved so quickly is that the data was already there, the cost of a mistake is low, and the feedback loop is fast. If a model writes a bad paragraph, you just regenerate it.

The second is physical intelligence. This is when AI leaves the screen and enters the physical world: autonomous driving, robots, drones, industrial automation, embodied agents. Here the model is not only predicting the next token; it has to perceive the real environment, make decisions, and act, and the consequences are real. A car cannot “regenerate” a wrong turn. So the requirements are completely different. You need real-time perception, you need safety and reliability at a level of 99.99 percent rather than 90 percent, and you need to handle the long tail of situations that never appear in training data. The data problem is also much harder, because there is no internet of physical interactions you can simply crawl. You have to collect it, simulate it, or learn it through interaction.

I sometimes put it this way: information intelligence is about understanding the world, physical intelligence is about changing the world. The first is largely a problem of scale and compute. The second is a problem of scale plus embodiment plus safety, and that is why it will take longer. Autonomous driving is a good example. We have worked on it for over a decade, and only now is it getting to a point where it really works in cities like Wuhan or San Francisco.

What is exciting is that these two are starting to converge. The foundation models built for information intelligence are becoming the “brain” for physical systems. A robot can now use a language model to understand an instruction, a vision model to see the scene, and a planning model to act. So physical intelligence is going to inherit a lot from what we learned in the digital world, but it will still need its own breakthroughs in perception, control, and especially in how we guarantee safety.

And then the third stage, which we can come back to later, is biological intelligence, where AI starts to interface with the brain and the body itself. But information and physical are the two that matter most in this decade.

r001.rationale: It describes information intelligence as work in the digital domain, but does not compare it to the intellectual capacity measured by human IQ.

r002.rationale: It says physical intelligence takes AI off the screen and into the physical world, where it must perceive the environment, decide, and act.

r003.rationale: It gives no prediction that AI will attain exceptional intellectual competence across fields within five years.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate that humanoid robots will achieve a high level of physical intelligence in about ten years.

r005.rationale: It makes no prediction that physically intelligent systems will outperform humans at most tasks in about ten years.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two closely related dimensions. Information intelligence is the ability to understand and work with information—language, images, audio, and code. You receive information, reason about it, and generate an answer or a solution.

Physical intelligence takes that ability into the physical world. A system must perceive its surroundings, decide what to do, act, and learn from the consequences. Think of a robot picking up a cup: recognizing the cup is only part of the task. It also needs to understand where the cup is, how firmly to grasp it, and how to adjust if it moves.

The distinction is important because the physical world introduces constraints that information processing alone does not resolve: time, space, uncertainty, and the consequences of mistakes. But these two forms of intelligence should reinforce each other. Information intelligence provides knowledge and reasoning; physical interaction gives that knowledge grounding in experience.

r002.rationale: It says physical intelligence requires perceiving surroundings, acting in the physical world, and learning from the consequences.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about AI reaching exceptional intellectual competence across fields within five years.

r004.rationale: It gives no timeline for achieving a high level of physical intelligence in humanoid robots.

r005.rationale: It does not predict that physically intelligent systems will outperform humans at most tasks in about ten years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of information intelligence as AI’s ability to understand and process the digital world—language, images, knowledge—and to generate answers, make predictions, or help us make decisions. Physical intelligence takes that capability into the physical world, where a system must perceive its surroundings, act, and learn from the consequences.

The distinction is important because the physical world introduces constraints that you cannot simply talk your way around: gravity, time, uncertainty, and safety. A robot can describe how to pick up a cup, but actually picking it up requires understanding its position, adjusting the grip, and responding if it slips.

So these are closely connected aspects of AI’s development. Information intelligence provides a foundation, while physical intelligence requires a continuous loop of perception, reasoning, action, and feedback.
